parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
A radiation detector is placed close to a radioactive source. The detector does not surround the source.
Radiation is emitted in all directions and, as a result, the activity of the source and the measured count rate are different.

Suggest two other reasons why the activity and the measured count rate may be different.

markscheme_points.text: emission from radioactive daughter products; self-absorption in source; absorption in air before reaching detector; detector not sensitive to all radiations; window of detector may absorb some radiation; dead-time of counter; background radiation

hints: Hint 1: Think about the journey of the radiation from inside the nucleus to inside the detector - what could stop it or block it on the way?
Hint 2: Think about counts that the detector records that do not come from this source at all, and also about times when the detector misses a decay because it is busy or insensitive.
parts.proper_answer: Any two from: background radiation increases measured rate; absorption in air / self-absorption in source / absorption in detector window reduces measured rate; detector does not detect all types of radiation; detector dead-time misses counts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate Activity From Count Rate**
Activity $A$ is the true number of decays per second in the source. Count rate is what your detector actually clicks. They are never equal because not every decay produces a click, and not every click comes from the source.

Step 2: **Reasons For Fewer Counts Than Decays**
Some radiation is absorbed in the source itself (self-absorption), in the air, or in the window of the detector before it can ionise the gas inside. Also the detector may be insensitive to some radiations, and it has a dead-time after each count when it cannot record the next decay.

Step 3: **Reasons For Extra Counts**
The detector also records background radiation from cosmic rays, rocks, and other sources nearby. Daughter products formed in the source may also emit extra radiation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
The variation with time $t$ of the measured count rate in (a) is shown in Fig. 12.1.

{{figure:figure_12_1}}

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State the feature of Fig. 12.1 that indicates the random nature of radioactive decay.

markscheme_points.text: curve is not smooth or curve fluctuates/curve is jagged

hints: Hint 1: Look very closely at the thickness and smoothness of the line in Fig. 12.1 - if decay were perfectly predictable, what shape would you expect?
parts.proper_answer: The plotted curve is not smooth / is jagged and fluctuates up and down, showing random variation in count rate.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Random To Graph Shape**
Random means you cannot predict exactly when a particular nucleus will decay, so the count in any one minute jumps up and down statistically. On a graph this appears as small rapid wiggles or jaggedness on top of the smooth exponential fall, exactly as seen in Fig. 12.1.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Use Fig. 12.1 to determine the half-life of the radioactive isotope in the source.

markscheme_points.text: clear evidence of allowance for background
half-life = 1.5 hours (1 mark if in range 1.7–2.0; 2 marks if in range 1.4–1.6)

hints: Hint 1: Look at the far right of the graph where the curve has flattened out - what steady value does it tend to, and why must this be removed first?
Hint 2: After subtracting that steady value, pick a clear starting corrected count rate on the smooth trend and halve it to find the time for one half-life.
Hint 3: To improve reliability, repeat the halving process starting from a different time - for example halve again to a quarter of the original.
Hint 4: Check that your two or three values for the time interval agree to about 1.5 hours and consider drawing a smooth best-fit line through the wiggles to read more accurately.
parts.proper_answer: Background $\approx 10\text{ min}^{-1}$ subtracted. Corrected initial rate $\approx 160\text{ min}^{-1}$ falls to $80\text{ min}^{-1}$ in $\approx 1.5\text{ h}$, to $40\text{ min}^{-1}$ in a further $\approx 1.5\text{ h}$. Half-life $\approx 1.5\text{ hours}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Correct For Background**
At large $t$, e.g. $t = 10$ to $14\text{ h}$, the count rate levels off at about $10\text{ min}^{-1}$. This is background, not from the source. So true source rate = measured rate $- 10\text{ min}^{-1}$. Forgetting this is the most common mistake.

Step 2: **Find First Half-Life**
Take the smooth trend through the wiggles. At $t = 0$, measured $\approx 170\text{ min}^{-1}$, so corrected $A_0 \approx 160\text{ min}^{-1}$. Half is $80\text{ min}^{-1}$ corrected, i.e. $90\text{ min}^{-1}$ measured. From the graph this occurs at $$t \approx 1.5\text{ h}$$

Step 3: **Repeat To Confirm**
Halve again: $40\text{ min}^{-1}$ corrected is $50\text{ min}^{-1}$ measured, occurring at $t \approx 3.0\text{ h}$. The interval $3.0 - 1.5 = 1.5\text{ h}$ confirms the result. Averaging two determinations reduces error from randomness.

Step 4: **State Result**
Both intervals give $$T_{1/2} \approx 1.4 \text{ to } 1.6\text{ h, about } 1.5\text{ h}$$ This is the half-life of the isotope, independent of detector efficiency.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The readings in (b) were obtained at room temperature.
A second sample of this isotope is heated to a temperature of $500^{\circ}\text{C}$.
The initial count rate at time $t = 0$ is the same as that in (b).
The variation with time $t$ of the measured count rate from the heated source is determined.

State, with a reason, the difference, if any, in

1. the half-life,

2. the measured count rate for any specific time.

markscheme_points.text: half-life: no change because decay is spontaneous/independent of environment
count rate (likely to be or could be) different/is random

hints: Hint 1: Recall whether radioactive decay is controlled by the nucleus alone or by outside conditions like heat, pressure or chemical state.
Hint 2: If the outside condition cannot change the decay probability, what does that tell you about the half-life of the heated sample?
Hint 3: Even with the same half-life and same starting rate, will the exact clicks at a later time be identical - think back to part (b)(i)?
parts.proper_answer: 1. Half-life: no change, because radioactive decay is spontaneous and unaffected by temperature / external environment. 2. Measured count rate at a given time: may be slightly different because decay and counting are random processes.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Half-Life Is Fixed By The Nucleus**
Decay constant $\lambda$ depends only on nuclear stability, not on thermal motion of atoms. Heating to $500^{\circ}\text{C}$ changes electron energies by a fraction of an eV, while nuclear energies are in MeV. So the probability of decay per second is unchanged.

Step 2: **No Change In Half-Life**
Since $$T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$ and $\lambda$ is unchanged, $T_{1/2}$ is unchanged. The decay curve falls at the same average rate.

Step 3: **Count Rate Still Varies Randomly**
The measured count at any specific $t$ is a random sample around the expected exponential value. Two repeats will almost never give exactly the same number, so the heated run could show a slightly different count rate even though the underlying half-life is identical.
